correctness.rationale: Independently reconstructed the 30-vertex cubic incidence graph with girth8, diameter4 and 45 edges; bipartite distance parity excludes same-side endpoints for odd length5. The S6 action is transitive on the two ordered point-to-matching distance types, with counts 45 incident, 180 nonincident and reversed copies. For representatives, constructed all positive-step length-five endpoint-localized tuples and signed smooth-point deletion matrices ∂3:C3→C2 and ∂4:C4→C3, with ∂3∂4=0. Independently recomputed at distance1 (C2,C3,C4)=(8,36,56), ranks(∂3,∂4)=(8,28), nonzero ∂4 Smith factors 1^28; at distance3 (14,45,40), ranks(14,27), ∂4 Smith factors 1^27. Because im∂4 is primitive in free C3 and contained in ker∂3, ker∂3/im∂4 is torsion-free, of rank zero or four. Summing 2×180×4 proves Z^1440; this is stronger than matching F2 dimensions. The finite enumerations are mathematically exhaustive for this one finite graph, not a sample or a general theorem for all girth-eight graphs.

value.rationale: Determining actual integer magnitude homology at the first nonvanishing second-off-diagonal girth-eight boundary for the unique (3,8)-cage is a natural exact invariant, not an arbitrary tiny graph exercise. Existing F2 data leave integral freeness, rational rank and possible odd-prime torsion unknown. Exhaustive signed Smith computations resolve these precise arithmetic questions, providing an all-characteristic refinement with no claim to solve higher magnitude homology.
residual_risks: The contribution is a single finite natural invariant (integral torsion), not a new general magnitude-homology theorem; the earlier F2 numerical result is explicitly prior art.

final_claim: For the Tutte–Coxeter incidence graph of 15 two-subsets and 15 perfect matchings of six symbols, the integral bidegree-(3,5) magnitude homology is Z^1440. Each ordered distance-three opposite-part endpoint pair contributes Z^4, each incident opposite-part pair contributes zero, and same-part groups vanish; in particular no integral torsion occurs.
